chapter: Paris scene and a visit home, 1937-39
title: Home in New York 1938-39: no Black bands and Harlem poverty
summary: Visiting home he felt Black jazz bands were being blocked out in favour of Goodman and Harry James and saw poverty in Harlem, after becoming Europeanized.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Now, we are in Paris and I said, I think I'd better go and see my people so, I come home. After seeing my mother and everything, I said, well -- but, while I was there it seemed, I felt that there was no more Negro bands playing jazz. They Blocked them out. All I was hearing was Benny Goodman and Harry James and Charlie Shivack and these people are great jazz kings and they said, well, we are swingin now and we've been swinging it hearing people swing; since I was a baby, I cut my teeth on / that's what Jelly Roll "Half cock that mute and Morton says/ swing that melody." That's what he said. In other words, carry that strong lead. So, I come back and I said, well, nobody was working.

This was around '38 and '39. I had been used to working and my attitude had changed, I had become Europeanized. I saw things from a different perspective. Why wasn't this man getting what he should get? Coleman Hawkins, he had been over in Europe and he stayed there a long time and they was having jam sessions but the people weren't getting paid and I saw poverty all in Harlem. When I left they were coming out from under
that era of poverty and they were trying to do things good and downtown, Birdland was moving nicely and things like that but when I come back it seemed like --
